question: What is the main virus that causes COVID-19?
explanation: COVID-19 stands for coronavirus disease 2019, and it is caused by the specific virus called Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which part of the COVID-19 virus helps it attach to human cells?
explanation: Think of the spike proteins as tiny crowns on the outside of the virus that latch onto human cells to start an infection. Great job! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which human cell receptors does SARS-CoV-2 mainly latch onto?
explanation: ACE2 receptors are found in large amounts in our lung tissue, making them the main doorway for the virus to enter the body. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the main danger of a cytokine storm in severe COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.B: Severe tissue damage from a hyperactive immune response
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of taste and smell
options.D: Complete shut down of bone marrow white blood cell production

explanation: A cytokine storm happens when the immune system goes into overdrive, flooding the lungs with chemicals that end up harming healthy tissue. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which symptom is uniquely linked to COVID-19 compared to many other common respiratory infections?
explanation: While many bugs give you a cough and fever, suddenly losing your sense of taste or smell is a classic sign of COVID-19. Well spotted! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: A patient has a breathing rate of 32 breaths per minute and an oxygen level of 91% on room air. How is this classified?
explanation: An oxygen level below 94% along with fast breathing means the patient is struggling and needs urgent care. You can totally master this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why do hospitals immediately isolate patients showing respiratory symptoms?

options.A: To speed up the administration of intravenous fluids
options.B: To reduce the cost of diagnostic testing supplies
options.C: To prevent transmission to staff and other patients
options.D: To allow patients to sleep without hospital noise

explanation: Isolating patients right away stops airborne droplets from spreading to other vulnerable people in the clinic. Smart nursing practice! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: What does 'silent hypoxia' mean in COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A complete absence of lung sounds during stethoscope auscultation
options.B: Normal breathing rates paired with severe panic attacks
options.C: Elevated carbon dioxide levels despite normal oxygen saturation
options.D: Dangerously low blood oxygen levels without the feeling of breathlessness

explanation: Some patients have critically low oxygen on monitors yet feel completely fine, which can be tricky and dangerous. Good to know for clinicals! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why are awake COVID-19 patients sometimes asked to lie on their stomachs (prone positioning)?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for oxygen therapy
options.B: It makes it easier to insert nasogastric feeding tubes
options.C: It improves lung expansion and oxygen exchange
options.D: It prevents patients from developing pressure ulcers

explanation: Proning helps open up parts of the lungs that usually get squished, helping the patient breathe much better. Every day you're building clinical skills! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What type of medicine is often given to hospitalized COVID-19 patients to prevent blood clots?
explanation: COVID-19 can make the blood more likely to clot, so doctors routinely prescribe blood thinners (anticoagulants) to keep patients safe. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What do we call health issues that linger for weeks or months after recovering from COVID-19?
explanation: When symptoms stick around long after the initial infection is gone, it's known as Long COVID. You're making steady progress! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which of these is a very common complaint from people dealing with Long COVID?

options.B: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: Total loss of long-term childhood memories

explanation: Many patients struggle with extreme tiredness and trouble focusing long after testing negative. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which mask must nurses wear during procedures that generate aerosols on COVID-19 patients?
explanation: Procedures that kick tiny droplets into the air require a tight-fitting N95 mask to keep you safe. Safety first in nursing! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which of these actions is WRONG when trying to stop the spread of respiratory viruses in a hospital?

options.A: Reusing disposable single-use gloves between multiple patients
options.B: Ensuring proper room ventilation in clinical spaces
options.C: Performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact

explanation: Single-use gloves are meant for one patient only! Reusing them is a sure way to spread germs around. You'd never make that mistake! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the main goal of getting widespread COVID-19 vaccinations?

options.A: Prevention of all future bacterial lung infections
options.B: Prevention of severe disease, hospitalization, and death
options.C: Complete eradication of all human coronaviruses worldwide
options.D: Immediate elimination of the need for hand washing

explanation: Vaccines help train your immune system so that even if you catch the virus, you are much less likely to get severely sick or end up in the hospital. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: How should a nurse best handle a patient who is hesitant about taking a vaccine?

options.A: Use empathetic communication and provide clear, factual information
options.B: Insist that vaccination is mandatory without discussion
options.C: Ignore their concerns and focus only on willing patients
options.D: Warn them that refusal will result in legal penalties

explanation: Listening patiently and addressing fears with kindness and facts is the best way to build trust. Great nursing communication! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)
